Twenty Sixth Indian Antarctic Expedition 2006-2008
Ministry of Earth Sciences, Technical Publication No. 24, pp 321-342
Ice Core Drilling in the Central Dronning Maud Land
and Snow Studies in the Larsemann Hills Region:
Field Activities and Initial Results
Meloth Thamban1 and P. K. Shrivastava2
1National Centre for Antarctic and Ocean Research
Earth System Science Organization (ESSO),
Ministry of Earth Sciences (Government of India)
Headland Sada, Vasco-da-Gama, Goa - 403 004 INDIA
2Geological Survey of India (Polar Studies Division), NH-5P, N.I.T.
Faridabad - 121001 INDIA
ABSTRACT
During the 26th Indian Scientific Expedition to Antarctica (ISEA), two shallow
ice cores were recovered from different sites in the Nivlisen ice shelf, north of the
Schirmacher Oasis. While the IND-26/B6 ice core (70º11’57.4" S latitude and 12 º
27  25.1" E longitude) was drilled up to a depth 75 m, the second core IND-26/B7
(70º 13.804 S latitude and 11º 55.738 E longitude) reached a depth of 55 m.
Additionally, 55 surface snow samples were collected along three transects in
different regions (Larsemann Hills region, Publications Ice Shelf and part of the
Amery Ice Shelf and the adjoining inland) within the logistic proximity of the
proposed new Indian station Bharati. Environmental analysis using multiple proxies
like ionic chemistry, trace elemental chemistry, micro-particle concentration, and
microbial diversity in the snow samples provided a wealth of scientific information
on the chemical and biological interactions of the snow deposits with the
atmosphere. The ice cores have been studied for the electrical conductivity
measurements (ECM) and stable oxygen isotope concentrations. The laboratory
data revealed large scale variability in the ECM and isotope parameters in the past,
suggesting significant changes in the environmental and climatic parameters during
the past several decades.
INTRODUCTION
The Antarctic continent itself makes up about 10% of the land surface
of the Earth with the combined area of the ice sheets and ice shelves being
about 14 x 10
6 km2 (Stonehouse, 2002). Ninety eight percent of Antarctica
322
is covered by thick ice sheets that contains about 90% of the world’s
‘permanent’ ice and 70% of its fresh water. The Antarctic Ice Sheet is
presently the largest and longest-lived ice mass on earth. The Antarctic ice
sheets in its present form are nearly 2.5 to 3 million years (Ma) old and
have an average thickness of 2,400 m and reaches a maximum thickness of
4,786 m. Additionally, the sea ice surrounding the Antartic continent has a
maximum winter extent of about 20 million km
2, the seasonal waxing and
waning of which is one of the largest seasonal signal on planet Earth. The
cryosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere in and around Antarctica are the
closely interactive components of a complex climate system, with global,
regional, as well as local influences. Therefore, Antarctica has a crucial
role to play in understanding the global change. Considering the physical
and dynamical enormity of the Antarctic ice sheet, it is essential to estimate
the glacier dynamics of this region for understanding the mass balance of
the global ice sheets. The undeniable finding of global warming scenarios
by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC, 2007),
necessitates the monitoring and evaluation of climate change effects on
glaciers and ice sheets of Antarctica. Studies on the ice sheet and its
contribution to world sea level rise are also vital to our understanding of
global change. The frozen archive of the Antarctic snow and ice is also an
invaluable source of information on climate and environmental history
(Stenberg et al., 1999). Further, Ice shelves around Antarctica are important
elements in the climate coupling of the Antarctic ice masses. The ice shelves
themselves have intensive interactions with the atmosphere (through ice
accumulation and ablation, radiation and albedo) and with the ocean
(through bottom melting and freezing, iceberg calving). Hence, ice shelves
are particularly sensible to climatic influences and changes.
Antarctic snow and ice represent one of the most pristine and high-
resolution environmental archive on the Earth for understanding the
environmental and climatic history of the globe in general and southern
hemisphere in particular. Ice cores drilled from carefully selected sites from
polar and tropical regions provide palaeo-environmental records on a
centennial, decadal, annual and even seasonal timescales (Blunier et al.,
1998; EPICA, 2006). The potential of ice cores for environmental
reconstruction and the lack of ice core data from the central Dronning Maud
Land (DML) encouraged Indian researchers to initiate ice core drilling
since the mid 1990s. The initial data from this region indicated the utility
of ice cores as high-resolution archives of climate change during the past
